questions.title: File Handling practice 1
questions.prompt: Which mode adds new text without deleting existing text?
questions.explanation: Append mode `a` positions writes at the end. Write mode `w` replaces existing contents, while read mode does not permit writing.

questions.title: File Handling practice 2
choices: To remove the newline around each line
To close the file
To convert each line to a number
To skip the first line
questions.explanation: File iteration keeps the newline character at the end of most lines. `strip()` removes it so `print` does not add an extra blank line.

questions.title: Trace File Handling
questions.code:
with open("courses.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("CS101\n")
    file.write("MATH120\n")

with open("courses.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.read())
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The `with` block owns the open file. When the indented block ends, Python closes it even if an error interrupted the work. The resulting output is 'CS101\nMATH120'.

questions.title: File Handling practice 5
questions.code:
with open("notes.txt") as file:
    text = file.read()
print(text)
questions.prompt: Why keep `file.read()` inside the `with` block instead of after it?
choices: The file is closed when the block ends, so reading after it fails
read() can only be called outside the with block
print() must be inside the with block
The file stays open forever either way
questions.explanation: `with` closes the file automatically when the block ends, so calling `file.read()` afterward raises a ValueError about I/O on a closed file. Do the reading inside; the *text* is an ordinary string you can freely `print` afterward. That is exactly what this version does.

questions.title: Write mode warning
questions.prompt: Before opening an existing notes file with mode `"w"`, what should a student check?
choices: Whether replacing the file contents is actually intended.
Whether `"w"` means read without changing anything.
Whether Python will append automatically if the file exists.
Whether `strip()` can restore the deleted text afterward.
questions.explanation: Mode `"w"` creates a new file or clears an existing one before writing. That is correct for replacement, but dangerous when the goal is to add new text. Use append mode for adding and read mode for inspection.

questions.title: Closing files safely
questions.prompt: A function reads a short text file and then returns a result. Which pattern protects the file handle?
choices: Open the file and rely on the program ending soon.
Use `with open(...)` so Python closes the file after the block.
Close the file before reading from it.
Read outside the block after the handle has closed.
questions.explanation: `with open(...)` gives the code a clear window where the file is open. When that block ends, Python closes the file even if an error happens inside. Reading after the block is too late because the handle has already been closed.

questions.title: Text encoding
questions.prompt: A program writes course names that may include accents or special characters. What should the file code specify?
choices: No encoding, because every computer chooses the same default.
Binary mode, because all text must be stored as raw bytes.
`encoding="utf-8"` for text the program controls.
`strip()` before opening so symbols are removed.
questions.explanation: Specifying UTF-8 makes text behavior predictable across machines. Without it, Python may use a system default that differs between computers. Encoding is chosen when opening the file; it is not fixed by string cleanup later.

questions.title: Choosing a file mode
questions.prompt: A program should add a new journal line without deleting old lines. Which mode fits?
choices: `"r"`, because reading automatically writes at the end.
`"w"`, because writing always preserves previous text.
`"x"`, because exclusive creation updates existing files.
`"a"`, because append writes after the existing contents.
questions.explanation: Append mode is designed for adding to the end of a file. Read mode does not write, and write mode replaces existing contents. Choosing the mode is one of the most important file-safety decisions.

questions.title: Missing file paths
questions.prompt: What should code expect when opening a file path supplied by a user?
choices: The path may be missing or blocked by permissions, so errors should be handled thoughtfully.
Python will create every missing folder automatically.
A wrong path returns an empty string instead of raising an error.
Permissions matter only when writing, never when reading.
questions.explanation: User-supplied paths can point to files that do not exist, folders that do not exist, or locations the program cannot access. Good file code decides whether to show a friendly message, ask again, or let the error reach a caller that can respond.

questions.title: Large file reading
questions.prompt: A log file may be too large to comfortably load all at once. What reading strategy is safer?
choices: Call `read()` several times and hope memory is enough.
Process the file one line at a time inside the `with` block.
Convert the file object to a tuple before scanning it.
Open the file in write mode so old lines disappear.
questions.explanation: Line-by-line reading lets the program handle one small piece at a time. That avoids holding the whole file in memory and keeps the file open only while it is being processed. It also pairs naturally with loops that count, filter, or search lines.
